newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thai stock rescue fund draws cool market response.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thai stock rescue fund draws cool market response.

text.p: A 50 billion baht ($1.92 billion) stock market support fund announced by the Thai Finance Ministry has drawn a lukewarm response from analysts who said the it failed to address concerns about weak economic fundamentals.
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Saturday that Thai commercial banks had vounteered to pool the fund to help shore up the stock market which tumbled to an eight-year low last week.

"Fifty billion baht is just a number game. It is difficult to imagine how are they going to raise the money while interest rates are high and banks are not flush with surplus cash," the head of equities at a local brokerage firm said.
Thai stocks suffered a hammering last week when investors dumped shares in reaction to heavy speculative attacks on the baht in foreign exchange markets. The baht later recovered.
On Friday, the composite SET Index closed at 561.19, down 44.24 points, or 7.3 percent, on the week. The index has plunged 15 percent this month and has lost 32.5 percent since January.

Amnuay said the government, which is facing lower tax revenues because of the slowing economy, also planned to cut its budget by trimming its 1997/1998 (October/September) expenditure by 26 billion baht to 982 billion.
The minister said he saw room for Thai banks to cut lending rates between one and two percentage points later this year to give cash-strapped businesses access to cheaper funds.

Graham Catterwell, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (Thailand), said the 50 billion baht fund may initially prop up battered stocks but it still did not deal with market fears about the economy.

"I assume stocks will go up if banks spend 50 billion baht in the market. But I am not in favour of rescue funds. The government worries a lot about market confidence rather than fundamentals. It forgets why the market goes down," he said.
Thailand's gross domestic product is projected by private analysts to grow about five percent this year, its slowest pace in a decade, against 6.7 percent in 1996 and 8.6 percent a year earlier.

A four-year property slump has also shaken finance companies saddled with large non-performing loans. The central bank has since April offered incentives for the country's 91 finance companies to consolidate through mergers.

Another analyst said Amnuay's signal for Thai banks to cut interest rates reflected his increased confidence in steering the economy out of its current downturn after the success last week in defending the baht against speculative attacks.

The foreign analyst said he agreed with Amnuay that Thai banks would face few risks in buying deeply discounted stocks. "We could see a drop in panic selling in the next few days, a signal that the market will go up again," he said, adding that some analysts were busy writing buyer reports on Sunday.
But analysts polled by Reuters said the latest rescue measure for the Thai bourse, rated the worst performer among more than 50 exchanges last month, left questions unanswered.
"Problems are not going to disappear. There are still a lot of questions about the property and finance sectors," he said.

As part of efforts to stabilise the stock market, the government said late last week Thailand Securities Finance Corp (TSFC), a semi-government company, would also float five billion baht of bonds to raise funds for refinancing troubled margin loan accounts carried by securities firms for three years.
The TSFC plan would help reduce cases of forced sales of stocks by heavily indebted investors and slow the bourse's fall. ($1 = 26 baht)
